issues.legal_issue: The absence of presidential assent did not permanently invalidate acquisition provisions in a state law that was within the legislature’s competence once the constitutional requirement for assent ceased to operate.
material_facts: The state legislature enacted the development law and it received the Governor’s assent, but it was not reserved for or given the President’s assent.
The law provided for acquisition for development purposes and made the Land Acquisition Act’s compensation principles applicable.
The constitutional provision requiring presidential assent was later removed.
issues.conclusion: The acquisition provisions were not nullities; the absence of assent prevented their enforcement only while the constitutional assent requirement remained in force, and the provisions became enforceable when that requirement ceased.
issues.legal_principle: Article 31(3), before its omission by the Constitution (Forty-Fourth Amendment) Act, 1978, postponed the enforcement of a state acquisition law pending presidential assent; it did not make the law a nullity. A law within legislative competence but temporarily unenforceable because of a constitutional restriction becomes effective when that restriction is removed, without reenactment: M.P.V. Sundararamier & Co. v. State of Andhra Pradesh. The court distinguished the treatment of post-constitutional laws under Article 13(2) discussed in Mahendra Lal Jain v. State of Uttar Pradesh. The legislature had competence under Entry 5 of List II, and the law provided for compensation principles through the Land Acquisition Act.

predicates.acquisition_law_challenge: A person challenged the enforceability of provisions authorising compulsory acquisition under a state law.
predicates.state_law_within_competence: The state legislature enacted the law within its legislative competence.
predicates.assent_requirement_later_removed: A constitutional requirement that had prevented enforcement without presidential assent later ceased to apply.

issues.definition: When a competent state law authorising acquisition was challenged for lack of presidential assent, and the constitutional assent requirement later ceased to apply, the acquisition provisions became enforceable.

issues.legal_issue: Constitutional provisions establishing municipal self-government and metropolitan planning did not displace a separate law empowering a development authority to undertake planned land development.
material_facts: The challenged law empowered a statutory authority to acquire land, form layouts, construct buildings, and provide related infrastructure for urban development.
The authority was not a municipality, although it included elected representatives and other members representing different interests.
Municipal bodies and metropolitan planning committees had distinct functions concerning local self-government and area-wide planning.
The law required government sanction for a development scheme and provided for municipal representations to be considered.
issues.conclusion: The development-authority law did not become inoperative or invalid when the constitutional provisions concerning municipalities and metropolitan planning came into force.
issues.legal_principle: Articles 243P, 243Q, 243W, 243ZE and 243ZF distinguish municipalities and metropolitan planning committees from specialised development authorities. Article 243ZF continues inconsistent laws relating to municipalities temporarily; it does not apply to a development-authority law that is not a law relating to a municipality. The functions of municipal bodies, including area-wide planning and municipal services, are distinct from the development authority’s work of acquiring land and carrying out building or engineering operations to form layouts. The court also relied on the distinct purpose of the development-authority law as described in its preamble and scheme.

predicates.challenge_to_development_authority_law: A party challenged a law authorising a specialised development authority on the basis of constitutional provisions concerning municipalities and metropolitan planning.
predicates.authority_is_not_municipality: The body exercising the challenged powers was a specialised development authority rather than an institution of municipal self-government.
predicates.development_functions_are_distinct_from_: The authority carried out land development operations distinct from the municipal functions of local self-government and area-wide planning.

issues.definition: A challenged development-authority law remains operable where the authority is not a municipality and its land-development functions are distinct from municipal functions.

issues.legal_issue: An ambiguous notification defining the territorial area of a development authority must be read consistently with the governing statute and the evident intention of including the relevant areas.
material_facts: The governing law included the city and areas where an earlier improvement law had applied, and allowed the government to add adjacent areas by notification.
The notification referred both to villages listed in a schedule and to an area within boundaries described in another schedule.
Those boundaries encompassed the listed peripheral villages as well as the city and the adjoining villages, including the villages where the acquired lands lay.
The development authority and the government had treated the broader area as within the authority’s territory in earlier development schemes.
issues.conclusion: The villages containing the acquired lands fell within the development authority’s territorial area, and the authority had jurisdiction to make a development scheme there.
issues.legal_principle: The definition in section 2(c) of the development-authority law included the city, areas where the earlier improvement law applied, and adjacent areas specified by notification. An ambiguous notification should be read to avoid absurdity and to give effect to its evident purpose; an omitted expression may be supplied only where there is clear necessity and the reason is found within the statute. The court relied on Padma Sundar Rao v. State of Tamil Nadu and considered Dr. Baliram Waman Hiray v. Justice B. Lentin and S.R. Bommai v. Union of India on the limits of supplying a casus omissus.

predicates.territorial_jurisdiction_challenge: A party disputed whether a development authority could undertake a scheme in the area containing the acquired land.
predicates.notification_is_ambiguous: The notification describing the authority’s territorial area used wording capable of more than one interpretation.
predicates.relevant_area_lies_within_notified_bound: The acquired land lay within the boundaries described in the notification when those boundaries were read consistently with the governing statutory definition.

issues.definition: Where territorial jurisdiction is challenged, an ambiguous notification establishes jurisdiction if the relevant area lies within its boundaries on a reading consistent with the governing definition.

issues.legal_issue: A time limit imposed by the Land Acquisition Act for its own final declaration did not invalidate a final declaration made under a separate acquisition procedure in a development-authority law.
material_facts: The development-authority law contained its own procedure for a preliminary notification and a final declaration.
The final declaration was published a few days more than one year after publication of the preliminary notification.
The development-authority law applied the Land Acquisition Act only so far as its provisions were applicable and used that Act for stages not covered by its own procedure.
issues.conclusion: The final declaration was not invalid merely because it was published more than one year after the preliminary notification.
issues.legal_principle: Section 36 of the development-authority law applies the Land Acquisition Act only so far as applicable. Where the development-authority law itself provides for the relevant acquisition stages, the corresponding provisions of the Land Acquisition Act do not apply. Accordingly, the time limit in section 6 of the Land Acquisition Act did not govern a final declaration made under the development-authority law. The court relied on Munithimmaiah v. State of Karnataka, which treated the development-authority law as a special and self-contained code.

predicates.development_authority_acquisition: The acquisition was undertaken as part of a development scheme under a law governing a development authority.
predicates.governing_law_has_its_own_preliminary_an: The law governing the development authority prescribed its own procedure for preliminary notification and final declaration.
predicates.land_acquisition_act_applies_only_to_unp: The governing law adopted the general acquisition law only for acquisition stages that its own provisions did not address.

issues.definition: A final declaration under a development-authority procedure is not invalid for missing a general acquisition-law deadline where the governing law supplies its own preliminary and final declaration stages.

issues.legal_issue: The Land Acquisition Act’s preliminary-notification, objection-inquiry, and final-declaration provisions did not govern acquisitions initiated and processed under the separate development-authority law.
material_facts: The development-authority law required a scheme to identify land for acquisition, publication of a preliminary notification, notice to affected persons to show cause, consideration of representations, government sanction, and a final declaration.
The authority issued notices and considered objections before submitting the modified scheme for government sanction.
The authority’s procedure did not provide for the personal hearing and inquiry prescribed by the Land Acquisition Act.
issues.conclusion: The acquisition was governed by the development-authority law’s own procedure; the absence of procedures required only by the Land Acquisition Act did not vitiate it.
issues.legal_principle: Sections 15–19 and section 36 of the development-authority law establish an acquisition process under that law, with the Land Acquisition Act applying only so far as applicable. The law’s notice and representation process is different from the personal hearing and inquiry under section 5A of the Land Acquisition Act; the latter requirements cannot be imported into the development-authority process. Article 254 does not apply merely because a state law incidentally touches a matter in the Concurrent List: the court relied on M/s. Hoechst Pharmaceuticals v. State of Bihar, Megh Raj v. Allah Rakhia, Lakhi Narayan v. Province of Bihar, and Munithimmaiah v. State of Karnataka in addressing legislative field and the nature of the development-authority law.

predicates.development_authority_acquisition: The acquisition was undertaken under a law governing a development authority as part of a development scheme.
predicates.governing_law_prescribes_its_own_acquisi: The governing law itself sets out the steps for identifying land, giving notice, considering representations, obtaining sanction, and declaring the land needed.
predicates.affected_persons_received_notice_and_rep: The authority notified affected persons and considered the representations received before proceeding with the scheme.

issues.definition: Where a development-authority law prescribes its own acquisition process and affected persons receive notice with their representations considered, procedures unique to the general acquisition law are not required.

issues.legal_issue: Changes in the extent and composition of a development scheme did not invalidate it where the statutory scheme-making and government-sanction procedures were followed and the required material was furnished.
material_facts: The authority began with a proposed scheme covering a smaller area, conducted surveys, added villages before the preliminary notification, and later reduced the area after considering objections.
The preliminary notification identified the lands proposed for acquisition and affected owners received notices to show cause.
The authority submitted the modified scheme, cost estimates, land particulars, and other required information to the government; it also answered requests for clarification.
The government granted sanction, initially on the Chief Minister’s approval subject to Cabinet ratification, and the Cabinet subsequently ratified the approval.
issues.conclusion: The scheme and government sanction were valid; changes made during scheme preparation did not make it vague or uncertain, and the required particulars had been furnished.
issues.legal_principle: Sections 15–19 of the development-authority law contemplate survey, scheme preparation, notice, consideration of representations, modifications, submission of specified particulars to the government, sanction, and final declaration. Changes and deletions during this process do not by themselves invalidate the scheme. The project map was not a document required to be furnished for sanction. Approval subject to Cabinet ratification was valid in the circumstances because the Cabinet subsequently ratified it under the applicable transaction-of-business process.

rule.if: development_scheme_acquisition and statutory_scheme_steps_completed and required_scheme_particulars_furnished and cabinet_later_ratified_conditional_approval

predicates.development_scheme_acquisition: The acquisition was undertaken to implement a development scheme prepared by a statutory development authority.
predicates.statutory_scheme_steps_completed: The authority prepared and notified the scheme, gave affected owners an opportunity to make representations, considered those representations, and submitted the scheme for government sanction.
predicates.required_scheme_particulars_furnished: The authority supplied the particulars required for government consideration and responded to requests for further information.
predicates.cabinet_later_ratified_conditional_appro: The executive approval was made subject to Cabinet ratification and the Cabinet subsequently ratified it.

issues.definition: A development scheme and its sanction remain valid where the prescribed scheme steps are completed, required particulars are supplied, and conditional executive approval is later ratified by the Cabinet.

issues.legal_issue: An owner is not entitled to equal withdrawal from acquisition merely because another owner received an unlawful or unjustified exclusion, although arbitrary exclusions may justify relief on an independent lawful basis.
material_facts: A substantial area initially proposed for acquisition was later excluded, without an adequate explanation of the extent or reasons for all exclusions.

The resulting acquired land included disconnected parcels and small pockets surrounded by land that was omitted or excluded, and the high courts found arbitrary and discriminatory inclusions and exclusions.
The authority had not adequately explained the differing treatment or the effects of the exclusions on the planned development.
issues.conclusion: The court rejected automatic equal treatment based on another owner’s potentially unlawful exclusion, but recognised that relief may be warranted where a lawful common criterion applies or arbitrary exclusions render the scheme unworkable; it directed further consideration of affected areas.
issues.legal_principle: Article 14 guarantees lawful equality, not repetition of an illegal benefit. A claimant must establish a just and lawful entitlement; an unlawful order in another person’s favour cannot ordinarily ground a right to the same order. If a valid policy or common criterion explains an exclusion and applies equally to the claimant, comparable relief may follow. Alternatively, arbitrary deletions may justify relief where they make the scheme impractical or inoperative. The court relied on Chandigarh Administration v. Jagjit Singh, Gursharan Singh v. New Delhi Municipal Committee, and State of Haryana v. Ram Kumar Mann.

predicates.acquisition_challenge: A landowner challenged the inclusion of the owner’s land in a compulsory acquisition.
predicates.another_owner_received_exclusion: A comparable or neighbouring owner’s land was omitted or released from the proposed acquisition.
predicates.exclusion_was_unlawful: The other owner’s exclusion was not supported by a lawful policy or valid criterion.
predicates.scheme_became_unworkable_after_exclusion: The extent and pattern of exclusions made the remaining development scheme impractical or incapable of orderly implementation.

issues.definition: A landowner does not automatically obtain another owner’s exclusion, even where that exclusion was unlawful, but scheme-wide unworkability may independently support relief.

issues.legal_issue: An acquisition for planned urban development may be preserved despite arbitrary exclusions when substantial implementation has occurred, provided affected landowners receive corrective review and additional relief.
material_facts: The authority had made awards, taken possession of substantial areas, laid out plots and infrastructure, and made allotments.

Many landowners had accepted the acquisition or received compensation, while the exclusions had created serious concerns about the practicality of development in certain villages and isolated pockets.

The court directed reconsideration of objections in areas where extensive omissions and deletions might make development illogical or impractical, and directed consideration of deleting isolated pockets unsuitable for self-contained layouts.
The court required the authority to offer affected petitioners a choice of developed land in lieu of compensation or a preferential plot in addition to compensation, subject to the stated conditions.
issues.conclusion: The acquisition was upheld subject to corrective review of specified areas and an option for affected petitioners to obtain developed plots or preferential allotments in addition to compensation.
issues.legal_principle: Where arbitrary and unexplained exclusions make an acquisition meaningless or unworkable, quashing may be necessary. However, where substantial possession and development have occurred and landowners and allottees would face hardship from quashing the whole acquisition, the court may preserve it subject to corrective measures. For acquisition for planned urban development, providing landowners a share in the developed land can make them beneficiaries of the scheme. The directions were tailored to the circumstances and were not declared general rules for regular acquisitions without irregularities.

predicates.planned_urban_development_acquisition: Land was acquired to create an organised urban residential development for members of the public.
predicates.substantial_implementation_occurred: The authority had taken possession of substantial land, formed plots or infrastructure, or made allotments, and affected owners had in many cases accepted the acquisition or received compensation.
predicates.arbitrary_exclusions_require_correction: Unexplained exclusions created a need to reconsider whether parts of the acquisition remained practical and suitable for the planned development.

issues.definition: Where substantial implementation of a planned urban development has occurred but arbitrary exclusions require correction, the acquisition may be preserved subject to review and additional landowner options.
